THE undersigned respectfully inform the
public, that, with the commencement of
the approaching Session of Congress they will
begin the publication of the "Congressional
Union and Appendix." The first will con-
tain a full and accurate history of the daily
proceedings of both branches of the national
legislature. It will be compiled with such care,
that every citizen who is interested in the pub-
lic affairs will find it complete synopsis of other
proceedings, and a ready book of reference up-
on all questions which come before them.
The second, the "Appendix," will contain
every speech which is delivered in the House of
Representatives and Senate during the session,
reported at length by full and able corps of
Congressional reporters, and revised before pub-
lication by the authors, whenever it is reques-
ted. These two works will be strictly impartial
and are intended to be as interesting and use-
ful to the man of business, and to the politician
of the one party, as of the other.

It may be said, without exaggeration, that
the next session of Congress is destined to be
one of the most important which has taken place
since the foundation of the government. It is
the longest session of the sessions which will
develope the general plan of the present admini-
stration. Its measures will stamp the character
of our institutions for years to come. Some of
the most important questions which are connec-

members into our public councils—every meas-
ure which affects the Oregon question—our re-
lations with Mexico—as well as the final decis-
ion on the revived Zoll-Verein treaty; these
and other measures which are more or less con-
nected with our foreign relations, will come un-
der the review of the approaching Congress.

relate to our internal concerns—the revision of Inc-
tariff—the adoption of the best mode for pre-
serving the public moneys—a variety of commercial
measures—perhaps the best system for regu-
lating the important interests of Texas—the In-
dian questions and questionable best sys-
tem for our navy—these and others will consti-
tute a mass of business which is calculated to
command much of the time of Congress, and
much of the attention of the people. They will
all be supported by the "Congressional Union."

ion, will, as usual, embrace an interesting varl-

We may regret the adoption of a system which, in its practical results, will, we fear affect injuriously all the great interests of the country. We cannot say that we are surprised at the facility with which, although formerly so vigorously resisted, it has been permitted, almost without struggle, to pass through the popular branch of Congress. May we not, however, look to the Senate for more deliberation on this radical change in the fiscal policy of the Government? May we not, indeed hope that that body, which, even as at present constituted, has nobly indicated its claim to be regarded as the truly conservative branch of our political system, will pause long before it gives its sanction to a measure, the principal recommendation of which seems to be that it is found in its simplest, and consequently in its most perfect form, in the most despotic governments.

We copy from the N. Y. Courier and Enquirer, the following synopsis of the most important features of the bill—

SEC. 1. Provides for the appointment of receivers general, to hold their offices for the term of four years, at the City of New York, at Boston and the city of St. Louis.

SEC. 5. Provides that receiving officers, of named exceptions, shall keep the money paid into them, without using it, until the same is ordered to be transferred or paid out.

SEC. 6. Provides that all receivers of public money within the District of Columbia shall whenever directed by the Secretary of the Treasury or Post Master General, pay the money received by them into the Treasury and that all Receivers of public money elsewhere shall pay the money received by them to the receivers general at least as often as once a week.

SEC. 10. Provides for the transfer of the public money upon the order of the Secretary of the Treasury.

SEC. 11. Makes it the duty of the Secretary of the Treasury, with much promptitude as the convenience of the public business and the safety of the public funds will permit, to withdraw to the balances remaining with the present depositors.

SEC. 12. Directs the manner in which the books shall be kept, &c. and provides that any loan of the public money or conversion of it to private use shall be adjudged an embezzlement of such money, which is declared to be a felony, punishable, on conviction, by imprisonment for not less than six months nor more than ten years, and fine equal to the amount of money embezzled.

SEC. 13. Provides that after the thirtieth day of June, one-third part of all duties, taxes, sales of public lands, debts, and sums of money accruing or becoming due to the United States, shall be collected in gold and silver; and from and after the thirtieth June, 1871, one other third part shall be collected in such currency; and after the 30th of June 1872, the remaining one third part shall be so collected; and from and after the last mentioned day all payments of government dues or of postage shall be made in such manner that all payments made by every officer or agent of the government, after the last mentioned period, to be in gold and silver only.

SEC. 14. Forbids any exchange of funds by any of the officers or agents of the government, other than an exchange for gold and silver; and directs every disbursing officer, when the means for his disbursements are furnished him in currency legally receivable, to make his payments in such currency, or when furnished drafts, to make his payments received for the drafts furnished, unless he can, in either case, exchange the means in his hands for gold and silver at par.

SEC. 15. Makes it the duty of the Secretary of the Treasury to issue and publish regulations to enforce the speedy presentation of all government drafts and prescribe the time in which all drafts shall be presented for payment and to guard, as far as may be, against those drafts being used or thrown into circulation as paper or medium of exchange.

SEC. 16. Fixes the salaries of the receivers general, &c. The receiver general at N. York to be paid $4,000 per annum; at Charleston $500, and at ST. LOUIS, $40, &c.
